The eight-ton rockets would be fired at an approaching asteroid with the hope of bumping it off course. If the asteroid was too close to Earth for this plan to work, the rockets would carry nuclear bombs to blow it up instead.
simplified:
Another idea to stop a dangerous space rock from hitting Earth is to destroy it with a nuclear bomb. This might sound like something from a movie, like the film Armageddon from 1998. But HAMMER, a NASA plan, is real.

Big rockets, weighing 8 tons, would be sent towards the space rock. The idea is to push it away from Earth. If the space rock was too close for that, the rockets would carry nuclear bombs to blow it up instead.
reference: Another way to stop an asteroid from hitting Earth is to destroy it with a nuclear weapon. This may sound like a film story, and it was actually in the 1998 film Armageddon. However, the Hypervelocity Asteroid Mitigation Mission for Emergency Response (HAMMER) is a real project from NASA. The plan was to send eight-ton heavy rockets towards an asteroid to push it away from its path. If the asteroid is already too close to Earth, the rockets could carry nuclear bombs to break it apart.

original: I work for a global IT company, but because their headquarters is in the States, I do all my work online from home. That means that I don't waste time commuting or making idle chit-chat with colleagues. I work on a project basis, and this flexibility is very valuable to me because it means that I can easily take some time off when my children need me to go to their school performances or if I need to schedule an appointment with the dentist. The downside is that without clear office hours, I tend to work well into the evening, sometimes skipping dinner to finish a task.
simplified:
I work for an international IT company. Their main office is in America, so I work online from home. This means I don't spend time travelling to work. I also don't chat much with colleagues.

I work on projects, and this is very helpful. I can easily take time off when my children have school shows or when I need to go to the dentist.

The problem is that I don't have set work hours. So, I often work late into the evening. Sometimes I miss dinner to finish a task.
reference: I work for a global IT company, but since the main office is in the United States, I do all of my work from home online. This is helpful because I save time: no travel and no small talk with coworkers. I work on different projects, and I really like the flexibility. I can take time off if my children have something at school or if I need to go to the dentist. However, there is a disadvantage. Without clear office hours, I often work late into the evening and sometimes miss dinner just to finish a task.

original: Around the 18th and 19th centuries two main ideas about dreams became popular. One was the idea that the things we see in our dreams represent things hidden from our conscious mind. Freud believed that if we understand what dreams are telling us, we can understand our hidden feelings and the problems they cause. However, the other theory was the opposite. It said that dreams are just a collection of random activity in the brain while it's organising memories and events from the day. When we wake up, we try to make sense of these random images and feelings and put them into some sort of story.
simplified:
In the 18th and 19th centuries, two main ideas about dreams were popular. One idea was that dreams show us things we don't usually know about ourselves. A man called Freud thought that if we understand our dreams, we can understand our secret feelings and the problems they cause.

But the other idea was very different. It said dreams are just random things happening in our brain when it's putting together memories and things from the day. When we wake up, we try to understand these random pictures and feelings and make them into a story.
reference: In the 18th and 19th centuries, two main ideas about dreams became popular. The first was that dreams show things that are hidden in our minds. Freud thought that by studying dreams, we can learn about our secret feelings and the problems they create. The second idea was the opposite. It said that the dreams are the result of random brain activity while it is sorting memories and events from the day. When we wake up, our brain tries to connect these random images and feelings into a story.

original: Underutilised items may seem useless to some, but could be an asset to others. With the advent of the internet, online communities have figured out a way to generate profit from the sharing of those underused assets. Using websites and social media groups that facilitate the buying and selling of second-hand goods, it is now easier than ever for peer-to-peer sharing activities to take place. And this is known as the sharing economy.
simplified: Things you don't use much might seem useless. But other people can use them. Thanks to the internet, people online have found a way to make money by sharing these things. They use websites and social media groups to buy and sell used items. This makes it very easy for people to share things with each other. This is called the sharing economy.
reference: Some things that are not often used may look useless to people, but they can be valuable to others. With the internet, online groups have found a way to make money by sharing unused items. With websites and social media pages that help people buy and sell second-hand goods, it is now easier for people to share items with each other. This is called the sharing economy.

original: Religion is important to Pi. Though his family is Hindu, he is curious about other religions and he makes friends with a Christian priest and a Muslim baker. To everyone's surprise, Pi declares himself to be simultaneously Hindu, Muslim and Christian. When his family and teachers ask him to choose just one religion, Pi refuses, saying 'I just want to love God'. From that moment, his family and teachers decide to let him make his own mind up about religion.
simplified: Religion is important to Pi. His family is Hindu, but Pi is interested in other religions. He becomes friends with a Christian priest and a Muslim baker. Everyone is surprised when Pi says he is Hindu, Muslim, and Christian at the same time. His family and teachers ask him to choose only one religion. But Pi says no. He says, 'I just want to love God'. After that, his family and teachers let him choose his own religion.
reference: Religion is very important to Pi. His family is Hindu, but he is also interested in other religions. He becomes friends with a Christian priest and a Muslim baker. To everyone's surprise, Pi says that he is Hindu, Muslim, and Christian at the same time. When his family and teachers tell him to choose only one religion, Pi refuses and says, "I just want to love God." After that, his family and teachers allow him to decide for himself about religion.

original: Blek le Rat started out painting rats on the walls of his home city, Paris. Nowadays, he tries to make people think about different social issues and problems. He paints pictures of homeless people in big cities to encourage residents to think about the problem of homelessness.
simplified: Blek le Rat began painting rats on walls in his city, Paris. Today, he wants people to think about social problems. He paints homeless people in big cities to make people think about homelessness.
reference: Blek le Rat was known for painting rats on the walls of Paris, his home city. Nowadays, his art focuses on social issues and problems. For example, he paints images of homeless people in big cities to make residents think more about the issue of homelessness.

original: The first is DART – the Double Asteroid Redirection Test. Plans are scheduled to test DART on the moon of an asteroid called Didymos. 'Didymoon' is 150 metres wide, orbiting its 800-metre mother, and hopefully the impact of DART will knock it out of its orbit enough for Earth-based telescopes to pick up.
simplified:
First, there is DART. This is a test to change the path of an asteroid.

Scientists plan to test DART on a small moon that goes around an asteroid called Didymos. This small moon is called 'Didymoon'. It is 150 metres wide. It goes around a bigger asteroid, which is 800 metres wide.

They hope DART will hit Didymoon and push it a little bit. This way, telescopes on Earth can see the change in its path.
reference: The first project is called DART-the Double Asteroid Redirection Test. Scientists plan to test it on the moon of an asteroid called Didymos. This moon, called "Didymoon," is 150 metres wide and goes around its larger parent asteroid, which is 800 metres wide. The hope is that the impact of DART will move Didymoon slightly out of its orbit so that telescopes on Earth can detect the change.

original: Faith47 is from Cape Town in South Africa. She paints big, colourful pictures of people and animals and likes to explore different locations. Her work is found on pavements, in empty factories and on abandoned cars. She likes the fact that most street art is temporary and will soon be removed by weather or cleaners from the city council. For her, this reflects how life is full of change with its cycle of endings and new beginnings.
simplified: Faith47 is from Cape Town in South Africa. She paints big, colourful pictures of people and animals. She also likes to paint in different places. You can see her art on sidewalks, in old factories, and on cars that no one uses. She likes that most street art does not last forever. The rain or city workers often remove it. For her, this shows that life always changes. Things end, and new things begin.
reference: Faith47 is an artist from Cape Town, South Africa. She paints big, colourful images of people and animals and enjoys working in many different places. Her art can be seen on pavements, in empty factories, and on abandoned cars. She likes that most street art is temporary and will eventually disappear because of the weather or city cleaners. For her, this shows that life is always changing, with endings and new beginnings.

original: When Gabriela became aware of the cultural differences between her and her team, she took the initiative to have an open conversation with them about their feelings about her leadership. Pleased to be asked for their thoughts, Gabriela's team openly expressed that they were not used to being told what to do. They enjoyed having more room for initiative and creative freedom. When she told her team exactly what she needed them to do, they felt that she didn't trust them to do their job well. They realised that Gabriela was taking it personally when they tried to challenge or make changes to her decisions, and were able to explain that it was how they'd always worked.
simplified: Gabriela understood the cultural differences between her and her team. She decided to talk openly with them about how they felt about her leading them. The team was happy she asked for their ideas. They said they were not used to being told what to do. They liked to have more freedom to start new things and be creative. When Gabriela told them exactly what to do, they felt she didn't trust them to do their job well. They understood that Gabriela felt bad when they questioned her ideas or changed them. They explained that this was how they always worked.
reference: When Gabriela noticed the cultural differences between her and her team, she decided to have an open conversation with them about her leadership. The team was happy to share their thoughts and explained that they were not used to being told exactly what to do. They enjoyed having more space for initiative and creativity. When Gabriela gave them strict instructions, they felt she did not trust them to do their jobs well. They also realised that Gabriela was taking it personally when they challenged her decisions. They explained that this was the normal way they worked.

original: People might not realise they are part of the disposable clothing problem because they donate their unwanted clothes to charities. But charity shops can't sell all those unwanted clothes. 'Fast fashion' goes out of fashion as quickly as it came in and is often too poor quality to recycle; people don't want to buy it second-hand. Huge quantities end up being thrown away, and a lot of clothes that charities can't sell are sent abroad, causing even more economic and environmental problems.
simplified:
People might not know they are part of the problem with too many clothes being thrown away. They give their unwanted clothes to charity shops. But these shops cannot sell all the clothes.

"Fast fashion" clothes are made quickly and cheaply. They go out of style very fast and are often too poor quality to recycle. So, people do not want to buy them used. Many clothes are thrown away. Also, many clothes that charity shops cannot sell are sent to other countries. This causes more problems for money and nature.
reference: People don't realise they are part of the problem of disposable clothing because they give their unwanted clothes to charity shops. However, these shops cannot sell everything. Fast fashion quickly goes out of style and is often too low in quality to recycle, so people don't want to buy it second-hand. As a result, a large amount of clothes are thrown away, and many that charities cannot sell are sent to other countries, which creates more economic and environmental problems.

original: According to Campbell, the hero at first refuses the call to adventure, but a mentor appears who helps them and they decide to 'cross the threshold' and travel into the 'special world' where the adventure happens. The next stage consists of passing tests, fighting enemies and meeting friends as the hero prepares to face their biggest challenge. For Luke the mentor is, of course, Obi-Wan, the friends are Han Solo and the robots R2D2 and C3PO and the enemy is Darth Vader inside the special world of the Death Star.
simplified: Campbell explains that heroes often don't want to go on an adventure at first. But then a helper appears. They decide to go into a new, special place where the adventure takes place. Next, the hero must pass tests, fight bad people, and meet friends. They get ready for their biggest problem. For Luke, Obi-Wan is the helper. His friends are Han Solo and the robots R2D2 and C3PO. Darth Vader is the enemy in the special world of the Death Star.
reference: According to Campbell, the hero first refuses to start the adventure. Then a mentor appears and helps them, so the hero decides to "cross the threshold" and enter the "special world" where the adventure takes place. In this world, Luke's mentor is Obi-Wan,  his friends are Han Solo and the robots R2D2 and C3PO, and his enemy is Darth Vader in this special world of the Death Star.

original: Have you ever dreamt of climbing Mount Everest or walking to the South Pole? If so, you're not alone. Every year, thousands of people try to climb the world's highest mountains or walk across continents. Unlike the explorers of the past who used maps and compasses, today's adventurers travel with modern technology like GPS and satellite phones. Many adventurers are nature lovers who use their travels to help raise awareness about a range of environmental issues, while others are keen to help people in need and raise money for charities.
simplified:

reference: In her old job, Gabriela worked in a culture with high power distance. In this culture, people respect power and authority, and everyone has a clear place. Leaders make the big decisions, and others do not usually question them. But her Swedish team was used to a low power distance culture. In this culture, employees often work with their bosses to solve problems and make decisions together. Leaders act more like coaches or mentors, encouraging independent thinking and expecting to be challenged.

Could the boy ride? he wondered. There was a whole load of trouble a good rider could get into out here, miles away from anyone. simplified: The two men looked to the north side of the land. It was very big. They could hardly see the fences from where they stood. A teenage boy might be bored and want to escape. But he couldn't walk away. Sam looked at the biggest horse. It was hitting the ground with its big feet. He wondered if the boy could ride a horse. A good rider could find a lot of trouble in this place, far from other people. But maybe someone who knew nothing about horses and wanted to leave his father would have even more trouble.
reference: The two men looked toward the north side of the land. It seemed to go on forever, and even the fences were hard to see from where they stood. No matter how bored or rebellious a teenage boy might feel, running away on foot was impossible. Sam's eyes moved to the biggest horse, which was kicking the ground with its heavy hooves. Could the boy ride it? he wondered. Out there, far from other people, a skilled rider could easily get into serious trouble. But perhaps a boy didn't know how to ride and only wanted to escape his father could face even greater danger.

original: Ed Stafford from the UK is the first person to walk the length of the Amazon River. He started by a small stream in the Andes mountains of Peru and arrived at the river's mouth in Brazil, two years and four months later, having walked 6,000 kilometres. The Amazon rainforest is home to poisonous snakes, crocodiles and jaguars, so Ed was in constant danger. Luckily, he survived with nothing worse than a few thousand mosquito and ant bites.
simplified:
Ed Stafford from the UK was the first person to walk from the start to the end of the Amazon River.

The Amazon rainforest has dangerous animals like snakes, crocodiles, and jaguars. So, Ed was always in danger. Luckily, he was fine. He only got many mosquito and ant bites.
reference: Ed Stafford, from the UK, is the first person to walk the whole Amazon River. He began at a small stream in the Andes mountains in Peru and finished at the end of the river in Brazil after two years and four months. He walked 6,000 km. The Amazon rainforest is home to poisonous snakes, crocodiles and jaguars. Ed was always at risk, but he survived with only many mosquito and ant bites.

original: In 2010, the planetary defence team at NASA had identified and logged 90 per cent of the asteroids near Earth measuring 1km wide. NASA thinks there are 50 more to find. But NASA says the 887 rocks they know about are not a big danger to our planet.
reference: In 2010, the planetary defence team at NASA had found and recorded 90% of the asteroids near Earth that are 1km wide. These are called 'near-Earth objects'. They are as big as mountains and are found within 50 km of Earth's prbit. original: Some people think writing your dreams down can open your mind to lucid dreaming. Lucid dreams are dreams where you're not only aware you're dreaming but you can make decisions to affect the events of your dreams. Then, instead of just working out the meaning of your dreams, you'll be creating them, though you might want to continue having some dreams that allow your subconscious to tell you what's on your mind!
simplified: Some people think that if you write down your dreams, you can learn to have lucid dreams. A lucid dream is when you know you are dreaming and you can control what happens. reference: Some people think that writing down their dreams can help them experience lucis dreaming. original: In Britain, the average person spends more than £1,000 on new clothes a year, which is around four per cent of their income. That might not sound like much, but that figure hides two far more worrying trends for society and for the environment. First, a lot of that consumer spending is via credit cards. British people currently owe approximately £670 per adult to credit card companies. That's 66 per cent of the average wardrobe budget. Also, not only are people spending money they don't have, they're using it to buy things they don't need. Britain throws away 300,000 tons of clothing a year, most of which goes into landfill sites.
simplified:
In Britain, people spend over £1,000 on new clothes every year. This is about 4% of their money. This number may seem small, but it shows two bigger problems for people and for nature.

First, many people buy clothes using credit cards. British adults owe about £670 each to credit card companies. This is 66% of the money they spend on clothes.

Also, people spend money they don't have, and they buy things they don't need. Britain throws away 300,000 tons of clothes every year. Most of these clothes go into big rubbish dumps.
reference: In Britain, people spend more than £1,000 a year on new clothes. This is about four per cent of their income. This may not seem like a lot, but it shows two serious problems for society and the environment. First, many people pay with credit cards. Second, people are not only spending money they don't have, but they are also buying things they dont need. Bridges are very important things which can allow cars, trucks and trains to cross rivers, mountain valleys or other roads. original: Both of these kinds of accidents are extremely rare, but boats and trains can cause a bridge to collapse for different reasons. reference: Both of these kinds of accidents are extremely rare, but boats and trains can cause a bridge collapse in different ways. For trains, the speed of the crash can break the bridge. Modern technology that finds weakness in bridges, safer working environments and better bridge designs can all help reduce these serious accidents.

original: The rover analyses the air around it periodically, and in 2014 it found the air contained another of the most basic organic molecules and a key ingredient of natural gas: methane. One of the characteristics of methane is that it only survives a few hundred years. This means that something, somewhere on Mars, is replenishing the supply. According to NASA, Mars emits thousands of tons of methane at a time. The level of methane rises and falls at seasonal intervals in the year, almost as if the planet is breathing it.
simplified: The rover checks the air regularly. In 2014, it found methane. Methane is a basic chemical and a part of natural gas. It only lasts for a few hundred years. This means something on Mars is making more of it. NASA says Mars releases thousands of tons of methane at one time. The amount of methane changes with the seasons, going up and down, almost like the planet is breathing.
reference: The rover sometimes analyses the air on Mars, and in 2014 it discovered methane, which is one of the basic organic molecules and an important part of natural gas. Methane can only last a few hundred years, so something on Mars must be making more of it. NASA says that Mars releases thousands of tons of methane at once. The amount of methane increases and decreases with the seasons, almost like the planet is breathing.

original: Early in her career, the psychologist Carol Dweck of Stanford University gave a group of ten-year-olds problems that were slightly too hard for them. One group reacted positively, said they loved challenge and understood that their abilities could be developed. She says they had a 'growth mindset' and are focused on what they can achieve in the future. But another group of children felt that their intelligence was being judged and they had failed. They had a 'fixed mindset' and were unable to imagine improving. Some of these children said they might cheat in the future; others looked for someone who had done worse than them to boost their self-esteem.
simplified:
Carol Dweck, a psychologist, once gave some ten-year-old children problems that were a little too difficult.

One group of children liked the challenge. They knew they could get better. She called this a 'growth mindset'. These children thought about what they could do in the future.

But another group of children felt bad. They thought people were judging how smart they were, and they felt like failures. She called this a 'fixed mindset'. They could not imagine getting better. Some of these children said they might cheat later. Others looked for someone who did worse than them to feel better about themselves.
reference: Early in her career, psychologist Carol Dweck from Stanford University gave ten-year-old children some problems that were a bit too hard for them. One group reacted well. They loved the challenge and believed they could improve their abilities. She says they had a 'growth mindset' and focused on what they can achieve in the future. Another group, however, thought their intelligence was being tested and felt they had failed. They had a 'fixed mindset' and could not imagine getting better. Some of these children even said they might cheat next time, while others compared themselves to children who had done worse to feel better.

original: At first, Pi is terrified of the animals and jumps into the ocean. Then he remembers that there are hungry sharks in the water around him and realises his only option is to climb back into the lifeboat. One by one, the animals in the lifeboat kill and eat each other, till only Pi and the tiger are left. Fortunately for Pi, the tiger, who he names Richard Parker, is seasick and has no immediate interest in eating him.

Inside the boat, the animals kill and eat each other until only Pi and the tiger remain. Luckily for Pi, the tiger, whom he names Richard Parker, feels seasick and is not interested in eating him right away.

original: Maybe dreams are the result of our mind organising the thoughts we have during the day, but they appear in dreams with symbolic meaning. reference: Dreams may happen because our mind is organising the thoughts we have during the day, but in dreams, these thoughts often appear as symbols. original: Businesses have caught on to the profitability of the sharing economy and are seeking to gain from making use of those underutilised resources. A business model that has rapidly risen in popularity sees companies providing an online platform that puts customers in contact with those who can provide a particular product or service. Companies like Airbnb act as a middleman for people to cash in on their unused rooms and houses and let them out as lucrative accommodation. Another example is Uber, which encourages people to use their own personal cars as taxis to make some extra cash in their free time.
simplified: Businesses have seen that the sharing economy can make money. They want to use things that are not used enough. A business idea that has become very popular quickly is when companies offer a website or app. This connects customers with people who can give them a product or service. Companies like Airbnb help people make money from their rooms and houses that they don't use. People can rent them out as places to stay and earn good money. Another example is Uber. It helps people use their own cars like taxis to earn extra money in their free time.
reference: Businesses now see that the sharing economy can make a lot of money. They want to use resources that are not being fully used. A common business model is when companies create an online platform that connects customers with people who can offer a product or service. For example, Airbnb acts as a middleman that helps people rent out their empty rooms and houses to earn money. original: Psychologist and 'growth mindset' proponent Carol Dweck spoke of the plasticity of the brain and our ability to develop skills and talents that we might not have been good at to start with. Many of us tend to focus our praise on the end result and seemingly innate talents, e.g. 'You really have an eye for details' or 'You have a real talent for organising events'. However, research suggests that by focusing on the process of how things are done – praising effort, experimentation and problem-solving strategies – we can encourage the development of new skills and the continued honing of talents.
simplified:
Carol Dweck is a psychologist. She talks about something called a 'growth mindset'. She says our brains can change. This means we can learn new skills and talents, even if we were not good at them before.

Often, we praise what people achieve or their natural talents. For example, we might say, 'You are good at details' or 'You are good at organising events'.

However, studies show a different way. If we praise *how* people do things – their hard work, trying new ideas, and how they solve problems – we can help them learn new skills. We can also help them improve their talents.
reference: Psychologist Carol Dweck, who supports the idea of a 'growth mindset', spoke about how the brain can change and how we can develop skills and talents, even if we were not good at them at firstt. Many people usually give praise for the final result or for natural talent, for example: "You are good at noticing details" or "You are great at organising events." But research shows it is better to focus on the process. By prarisising effort, trying new things, and problem-solving, we can help people build new skills and improve their talents.

original: Ed's walk would have been impossible without technology. He used a radio to ask the people of the rainforest for food and permission to cross their land. Many of them came to meet him and helped guide him through the most difficult terrain. As he walked Ed wrote a blog, recording his day-to-day experiences. He used the media interest in his trip to protest about the destruction of the rainforest and raise money for environmental and children's charities in Brazil and Peru.
simplified: Technology helped Ed a lot on his walk. He used a radio to talk to people in the rainforest. He asked them for food and if he could cross their land. Many people met him and helped him walk through the hardest parts of the land. While he walked, Ed wrote a blog about his daily experiences. News companies were interested in his trip. Ed used this to protest against cutting down the rainforest. He also collected money for groups that help nature and children in Brazil and Peru.
reference: Ed could not have completed his walk without technology. He used a radio to ask people in the rainforest for food and permission to cross their land. Many of these people met him and helped guide him through difficult areas. While walking, Ed also wrote a blog about his daily experiences. He used the media attention in his trip to protest against the destruction of the rainforest and to collect money for environmental and children's charities in Brazil and Peru.

original: In an attempt to inject some positivity into their feedback, many managers rely on sandwiching negative feedback between two positive comments. However, when feedback becomes such a routine, employees can start to perceive positive feedback as simply a form of sugarcoating the negatives, thus diminishing its value. Instead, positive feedback should not simply be seen as something to cushion the negative, but should be delivered so as to reinforce and encourage good performance.
simplified:
Many managers try to make their feedback more positive. They often put negative comments between two positive ones.

But if managers always do this, employees might think the good comments are just to hide the bad ones. This makes the good comments less important.

Good feedback should not just be used to make bad news softer. It should be given to show what is good and help people do even better.
reference: Many managers try to make feedback softer by using the "sandwich" method: they give a positive comment, followed by a negative one, and finish with another positive. But if this happens too often, workers may think that positive words are only there to hide the bad ones. This makes positive feedback less useful. Positive feedback should not just be used to cover the negatives. It should be given clearly to support the good work.

original: It was a fascinating talk and the speaker really hit the nail on the head with a couple of things. Take parental influence, for instance. How can we expect teenagers not to text while doing their homework when they witness their parents posting on social media while cooking the evening meal or waiting at a red light? She also made a valid point about people wanting to be in two or several places at once. So they switch back and forth between their real-life and online conversations. I see it all the time with my teenage daughter and her friends. They arrange to meet and then sit together in silence while each one engages in a different conversation online.
simplified:
The talk was very interesting. The speaker said some very true things. For example, think about how parents affect their children. Teenagers see their parents using social media when they cook dinner or wait at a red light. So, how can we ask teenagers not to text when they do homework?

The speaker also said something important. People want to be in many places at the same time. So they quickly change between talking to people face-to-face and talking online. I see this often with my teenage daughter and her friends. They plan to meet. But then they sit together quietly. Each friend is busy with a different online chat.
reference: The talk was very interesting, and the speaker made some excellent points. One example was about the influence of the parents. How can we expect teenagers not to text during their homework if they see their parents posting on social media while cooking or even at a traffic light? She also pointed out that people want to be in more than one place at the same time. So they switch between real-life and online conversations. I see this often with my teenage daughter and her friends. They meet up and then sit in silence while each one is busy with a different online conversation.

original: Gary Collins, an off-duty policeman, was watching the London riots on TV. He immediately recognised several people and cut his holiday short to help with identification. He ended up spending six months going through the CCTV film and managed to identify 190 people, many from their eyes alone. His help was of decisive importance in the investigation. Even with 200,000 hours of footage, facial recognition software managed to identify just one person.
simplified:
Gary Collins was a policeman. He was not working when he watched the London riots on TV.
He quickly saw some people he knew. He stopped his holiday early to help the police. He helped them find out who the people were.
He spent six months looking at CCTV videos. He found 190 people. He knew many of them just by their eyes.
His help was very important for the police investigation.
There were 200,000 hours of videos. But a special computer program could only find one person.
reference: Gary Collins, a policeman who was off for holidays, was watching the London riots on television. He immediately recognised several people and ended his holiday early to help identify them. He then spent six months looking at CCTV videos and managed to identify 190 people, many just from their eyes. His work was very important for the investigation. To compare, facial recognition software could only identify one person from 200,000 hours of video.

original: When Pi is 16, a new government is elected that his parents don't support. Worried about the future, Pi's parents decide to close the zoo and emigrate to Canada. reference: When Pi is 16, a new government comes to power, but his parents do not support it. They worry about the future, so they decide to close the zoo and move to Canada. Some of the animals are sold to North American zoos, and the family travels by ship to Canada with the rest of the animals. During the journey, a terrible storm hits, and the ship sinks. Sadly, Pi's family and the sailors all drown, but Pi survives in a lifeboat with a hyena, zebra, orang-utan and a big tiger.

original: Having good relationships is a big part of being happy. In one study, most happy people were found to have strong ties to friends and family and they made sure they spent time with them regularly. You also need at least one person who you discuss personal feelings with – called 'self-disclosure'. Just one person for a heart-to-heart is enough, together with a network of other relationships. It's not enough to have lots of friends just to do things with or chat to about music or football. That deeper connection is all-important. Some people need to learn how to listen effectively to others in order to develop stronger relationships.
simplified: Good relationships help us be happy. One study showed that most happy people had close friends and family. They spent time with them often. You also need at least one person you can talk to about your personal feelings. One person for deep talks is enough, along with other friends and family. It's not enough to have many friends just to do things with or talk about simple things like music or sports. That deeper connection is very important. Some people need to learn to listen well to others to make their relationships stronger.
reference: Good relationships are a big part of happiness. In one study, most happy people were found to have close connections with family and friends, and they spent time with them often. It is also important to have at least one person you can talk to about personal feelings. It is called "self-disclosure". One close person for heart-to-heart talks, plus a wider group of friends, is enough. Having many friends just for activities or small talk about things like music or football is not enough. A deeper connection is important. Some people also need to learn how to listen to others better so they can build stronger relationships.

original: As for news stories that make us think the world is an increasingly violent place, there is cause for some optimism too. Between the end of World War II and 1990, there were 30 wars that killed more than 100,000 people. Today there are still civil wars, but countries are mostly co-existing more peacefully than in the past. However, terrorism has shot up in the last few years and, since World War II, wars have killed many more civilians than soldiers. Even for civilians, though, the statistics are not all bad. Although deaths are nine times more likely to be a result of violent crime than political conflict, the global murder rate fell slightly, from 8 per 100,000 people in 2000 to about 5.3 in 2015.
simplified:
News often makes us think the world is very violent. But there is also good news.

From the end of World War II until 1990, 30 wars killed over 100,000 people each. Today, there are still wars inside countries. But most countries now live together more peacefully than before.

However, terrorism has increased a lot in recent years. Also, since World War II, wars have killed more ordinary people than soldiers. But even for ordinary people, the numbers are not all bad.

People are nine times more likely to die from violent crime than from wars. But the number of murders around the world went down a little. In 2000, 8 out of 100,000 people were murdered. In 2015, this number was about 5.3.
reference: When we read the news, it may seem like the world is becoming more violent, but there are also reasons to be hopeful. Between the end of World War II and 1990, there were 30 wars that killed more than 100, 000 people. Today, there are still civil wars, but many countries live more peacefully than before. Terrorism has grown in the last years, and since World War II, wars have killed more civilians than soldiers. But statistics are not all bad for civilians. Deaths are nine times more likely to come from violent crime than from political conflict, but the global murder rate has gone down, from 8 per 100,000 people in 2000 to about 5.3 in 2015.

original: Personally, I think it's fascinating to consider how we'll speed up our evolution as a species by augmenting our bodies. Imagine if you could implant a computer inside our brain! Soon we'll be able to do just that and enhance our mathematical ability, audiovisual perception and our memory, and this idea is only going to become more and more commonplace.
simplified: I think it's very interesting to think about how we can make ourselves better and change faster. Imagine putting a computer inside your brain! Soon we can do this. It will make our maths skills better, improve how we see and hear, and help our memory. This idea will become very common.
reference: I think it is very interesting to imagine how humans will evolve faster by adding technology to our bodies. For example, imagine having a computer inserted into our brain. In the future, this may be possible, and it could improve our maths skills, our hearing and sight, and our memory. This idea will probably become more and more common.

original: I'm a member of the Campaign to Stop Killer Robots. Forget the movie image of a terrifying Terminator stamping on human skulls and think of what's happening right now: military machines like drones, gun turrets and sentry robots are already being used to kill with very little human input. The next step will be autonomous 'murderbots', following orders but ultimately deciding who to kill on their own. It seems clear to me that this would be completely unethical and dangerous for humanity. We need to be very cautious indeed about what we ask machines to do.
simplified: I'm a member of the Campaign to Stop Killer Robots. Don't think about scary movie robots like the Terminator. Think about what is happening now: army robots like drones, robot guns, and guard robots are already killing people. Humans don't control them much. The next step will be robots that kill by themselves. They will follow orders, but they will choose who to kill. I think this is very wrong and dangerous for all people. We must be very careful about what we let machines do.
reference: I am part of the Campaign to Stop Killer Robots. Forget the picture from films of a scary robot like the Terminator. Look instead at what is happening now: military machines such as drones, gun turrets, and guard robots are already being used to kill with little control from humans. The next step could be fully independent "murderbots," which follow orders but also decide on their own who to kill. I believe this would be very wrong and dangerous for all people. We must be very careful about what jobs we give to machines.

original: Horror films love uninhabited places. This could be an abandoned hospital, a scary empty house or a ghost town. There's something about lonely, empty places. What was it like when people lived there? Why did they leave? Maybe it's also that they are so quiet, which can be very scary too. Of course, abandoned places are also handy for horror film directors in that it's more believable that you will have no phone coverage there either.
simplified: Horror films like empty places. These could be an empty hospital, a scary house, or a town with no people. There is something special about these quiet, empty places. What was it like when people lived there? Why did they leave? Their quietness can also be very scary. Empty places are also useful for horror films because it's easy to believe you can't use your phone there.
reference: Horror films often happen in empty places. These could be old hospitals, abandoned houses, or ghost towns. Such lonely and empty places make us think: what was it like when people lived there? Why did they leave? The slience also adds to the fear, because quiet can be very scary. For directors, abandoned places are also useful, as it seems realistic that there would be no phone signal there.

original: The majority of people believe that developing countries are in a terrible situation: suffering from incredible poverty, governed by dictators and with little hope for any meaningful change. But, surprisingly, this is far from the truth. The reality is that a great transformation is occurring. Over the past 20 years, more than 700 million people have increased their income and come out of poverty. Additionally, six million fewer children die every year from disease, millions more girls are in school and millions of people have access to clean water.
simplified:
Many people think that poor countries are in a very bad way. They believe these countries are very poor, have dictators, and things will not change. But this is not true. Actually, big changes are happening.

In the last 20 years, over 700 million people now earn more money and are no longer poor. Also, every year, six million fewer children die from sickness. Millions more girls can go to school, and millions of people now have clean water.
reference: Many people think that developing countries are in very bad conditions. They imagine extreme poverty, strong rulers who do not allow freedom, and no chance for change. But this is not the truth. In fact, a big change is happening. Over the past 20 years, more than 700 million people have escaped poverty by earning more money. Also, six million fewer children die each year from sickness. More girls are now going to school, and millions of people can drink clean water.

original: Wasfia has dedicated her life to supporting human rights and has witnessed numerous international humanitarian projects in her homeland to educate and train women and girls, but once too often they have been left with nothing when such projects have stopped running. Wasfia saw that Bangladesh needed to stand up for itself and so she brought together two of her passions, mountaineering and human rights, in order to try and change attitudes towards women in her country. She originally took up climbing while working on humanitarian campaigns in Tibet and Nepal, as in a coastal, primarily flat country like Bangladesh most people have never set eyes on a mountain. Her campaign seems to be doing the trick as fellow countrymen and women are sitting up and taking notice along with the rest of the world.
simplified:
Wasfia has spent her life helping human rights. She has seen many international help projects in her country. These projects taught women and girls. But often, when these projects finished, the women and girls had nothing left.

Wasfia thought Bangladesh needed to help itself. So, she combined two things she loved: mountain climbing and human rights. She did this to try and change how people think about women in her country.

She started climbing mountains when she worked on help projects in Tibet and Nepal. Bangladesh is a country by the sea and mostly flat, so most people there have never seen a mountain.

Her work seems to be succeeding. People in her country and around the world are starting to pay attention.
reference: Wasfia has spent her life helping people fight for human rights. In her homeland, she has seen many international projects that tried to teach and train women and girls, but often these projects ended with leaving them with nothing. Wasfia saw that Bangladesh needed to stand up on their own. She joined her two passions- mountain climbing and human rights, to change how people think about women. She first started climbing in Tibet and Nepal, because in Bangladesh, which is flat and near the sea, most people have never seen a mountain. Her campaign is working, as people in Bangladesh and around the world are paying attention.

original: In older horror films, when protagonists were in desperation, it was difficult or impossible for them to call for help or call the police. Mobile phones have made that situation a bit less believable now. What's the solution to maintain suspense? No phone coverage! If you're a hero in a horror film, it's almost certain that at a key moment, just when you absolutely need to call for help, you will not have any coverage at all. Or your phone battery will die just as you are making the call. Or both.
simplified:
In old scary movies, the main characters often couldn't call for help or the police when they were in danger.
Today, with mobile phones, this is harder to believe.
So, how do they keep the story exciting?
They make sure there's no phone signal!
If you are the hero in a scary movie, it's very likely that when you really need to call for help, your phone won't work.
Or your phone battery will run out when you try to call.
Sometimes, both happen.
reference: In old horror films, when the main characters were in trouble, it was hard or even impossible for them to call for help or contact the police. Today, with mobile phones, that probelm seems less realistic. So how do filmmakers keep the suspense? They use the idea of no phone signal. In many horror films, at the key moment when the hero needs to call for help, there is no signal. Or the phone battery will die just as thry make the call. Or sometimes both happen.

original: This horror film cliché was especially popular with horror films of the late 20th century. It starts with a group of teenagers all enjoying themselves, and it ends with everyone dead except one girl. At the beginning the girl is usually innocent, shy and not particularly strong. By the end, she has become the toughest and most resourceful person in the world. The last girl almost always wins in the end.
simplified:
This is a common story in horror films. It was very popular in films from the late 1900s.
It starts with some teenagers having fun. But then everyone dies, except for one girl.
At first, this girl is usually good, shy, and not very strong.
But by the end, she becomes very strong and clever.
This last girl usually wins in the end.
reference: This horror film cliché was especially popular in the late 20th century. The story usually begins with a group of teenagers having fun, but it ends with all of them dead except for one girl. At first, this girl is often  quite, shy and not very strong. By the end, she becomes brave, smart, and strong enough to survive. The "last girl" almost always win the danger at the end.

original: Your manager stops you and says she needs to have a word about your performance in the recent project. You worry about it all weekend, wondering what you might have done wrong. When you step into her office on Monday morning she begins by praising you for the good work you've done on the project, and you wonder if this is the obligatory praise that starts off the typical 'feedback sandwich'. You know how the feedback sandwich goes: say something nice, say what you really want to say, say something nice again.
simplified:
Your manager stops you. She says she needs to talk about your work on the last project. You worry all weekend, thinking about what mistakes you might have made.

On Monday morning, you go into her office. She starts by saying good things about your work on the project. You think, 'Is this just the usual good words before she says something bad?' This is like a 'feedback sandwich'. You know how it works: first, she says something good. Then, she says the real problem. Finally, she says something good again.
reference: Your manager stops you and says she wants to talk to you about your work on the last project. You worry about it all weekend, thinking you may have done something wrong. On Monday, you go into her office and she starts by saying good things about your work. You are not sure if this is just the usual "feedback sandwich". The feedback sandwich goes like this: You say somthing nice, then say something you really want to say (usually a criticism), then say something nice again.

original: Overall, more people are learning English than the other languages combined and English is spoken in the highest number of countries. However, Chinese has by far the greatest number of native speakers. There seems to be little correlation between how many native speakers there are of a language and the number of learners, but there is a stronger link between the number of learners and how many countries have speakers.
simplified:
More people learn English than all other languages together. English is also spoken in the most countries.

However, Chinese has the most native speakers.

The number of people who speak a language from birth does not seem to be very connected to how many people learn it. But there is a stronger connection between how many people learn a language and how many countries speak it.
reference: More people are learning English than all other languages, altogether,  and English is the most spoken language in many countries. But Chinese has the largest number of native speakers. There is not much link between how many native speakers a language has and how many people learn it. Instead, there is a stronger link between how many people learn a language and how many countries use it.

original: A fast-paced, foot-tapping rock album, Born in the USA's lyrics nevertheless carry emotional weight. Behind the catchy rock melodies that drive these powerhouse classics are stories of the dark side of the American dream. Many tracks deal with the struggles of hard-working ordinary people and the bitterness and anger they feel as life doesn't bring them riches or glory. The song Glory Days, for example, is about people in a small town looking back at when they were young and had the world at their feet while Downbound Train tells the story of a young man whose life is ruined when he loses his job. It's not hard to imagine that the artist is channelling real people he knew and the life he might have had if he hadn't become a star. The album will leave you in no doubt of the unique and extraordinary talent of the Boss.
simplified:
"Born in the USA" is a rock album with quick, exciting music. But the words in the songs have deep feelings. The famous songs have easy-to-remember rock tunes. But they tell stories about the difficult parts of the American dream.

Many songs are about the problems of normal people who work hard. They feel sad and angry because life does not give them money or fame. For example, the song "Glory Days" is about people in a small town. They remember when they were young and felt like they could do anything. "Downbound Train" tells the story of a young man whose life becomes bad when he loses his job.

It is easy to think that the artist writes about real people he knew. He also writes about the life he might have lived if he was not famous. This album will clearly show you that The Boss has a special and amazing talent.
reference: Born in the USA is a fast rock album with strong rhythms, but its lyrics also convey deep feelings. Behind the catchy music are stories about the dark side of the American dream. Many songs talk about the hard lives of working people and their anger when life does not give them money or successs. For example, Glory Days is about small-town people remembering their youth, while Downbound Train tells of a young man whose life falls apart after losing his job. It is easy to think the singer is using the voice of the real people he knew, and the life he might have lived without fame. The album clearly shows the great talent of "the boss".

original: Best-selling author Terrie Sharp knows how to tell a good story or two, having twice won the Olive Crime Writer Award. Born on the housing estate with the highest crime rate in Glasgow, she learned to keep quiet, stay out of trouble and how to open car doors with a knife. Luckily, she only used her knowledge to write her novels and she's not so quiet these days, appearing on popular daytime shows like Police Today and at writing conferences throughout the UK.
simplified:
Terrie Sharp is a very popular writer. She is good at telling stories and has won the Olive Crime Writer Award two times.

She grew up in an area of Glasgow with a lot of crime. There, she learned to be quiet, avoid problems, and how to open car doors with a knife.

Fortunately, she only used this knowledge for her books. Now, she is not quiet. She appears on popular TV shows, like 'Police Today', and goes to writing events all over the UK.
reference: Terrie Sharp is a best-selling author who knows how to tell exciting stories. She has won the Olive Crime Writer Award twice. She grew up on a housing estate in Glasgow that had the highest crime rate in the UK. There, she learned to stay quiet, avoid trouble, and even open car doors with a knife. Luckily, she only used this in her books. Nowadays, she is not that quite, she often appears on TV shows like Police Today and speaks at writing conferences across the UK.

original: In the 1950s, Central American commercial banana growers were facing the death of their most lucrative product, the Gros Michel banana, known as Big Mike. And now it's happening again to Big Mike's successor – the Cavendish. With its easily transported, thick-skinned and sweet-tasting fruit, the Gros Michel banana plant dominated the plantations of Central America. United Fruit, the main grower and exporter in South America at the time, mass-produced its bananas in the most efficient way possible: it cloned shoots from the stems of plants instead of growing plants from seeds, and cultivated them in densely packed fields.
simplified:
In the 1950s, banana farmers in Central America had a big problem. Their most important product, the Gros Michel banana (also called Big Mike), was dying. Now, the same problem is happening again to the Cavendish banana, which replaced Big Mike.

The Gros Michel banana was easy to move, had a thick skin, and tasted sweet. It was the main banana grown on farms in Central America.

United Fruit was the biggest company that grew and sold bananas in South America at that time. They grew many bananas in the fastest way possible. They made new plants from parts of old plants, not from seeds. They grew these plants very close together in big fields.
reference: In the 1950s, banana growers in Central America saw their most valuable banana, the Gros Michel (called Big Mike), begin to die out. Now the same problem is happening to Big Mike's replacement—the Cavendish banana. The Gros Michel was very popular because it was sweet, had a thick skin, and was easy to transport. It was the main banana grown in Central America. United Fruit, the biggest company at the time, grew bananas in the most efficient way: instead of using seeds, they cloned shoots from stems and planted then close together in larger fileds.

original: Lewis would like to see the number of marine protected areas in the world increase from 3 per cent to 10 per cent in an attempt to reverse the damage caused by human activity such as overfishing, polluting and littering. During his expeditions, Lewis has witnessed this environmental destruction first-hand. He's swum over coral reefs bleached by the increase in water temperature, and observed underwater deserts beneath the shallow waters of the Red Sea, devoid of life and strewn with plastic. Pugh believes that nature can recover if it is given space to do so, but the clock is ticking. If we don't start looking after our seas, we may soon have an unsolvable problem on our hands.
simplified:
Lewis wants more parts of the sea to be protected. He wants this number to grow from 3% to 10%. This is to stop the damage caused by people, such as too much fishing, making the water dirty, and throwing rubbish.

Lewis has seen this damage to nature himself during his journeys. He has swum over coral reefs that are white because the water is too warm. He has also seen places under the sea in the Red Sea that are like deserts, with no life and full of plastic.

Pugh believes nature can get better if we give it space. But there is not much time. If we don't start taking care of our seas, we might soon have a problem we cannot solve.
reference: Lewis wants to see the number of marine protected areas in the world increase from 3% to 10%. He believes this can help repair the damage caused by people, such as overfishing, pollution, and throwing rubbish into the sea. On his journey, Lewis has seen this destruction himself. He has swum over coral reefs that turned white becaurse of warmer water and seemed empty underwater deserts in the Red Sea, with no life and loads of plastic. Pugh thinks nature can recover if we give it space, but time is running out. If we dont take care of our seas now, they problem may soon be impossible to solve.

original: At Girox Foods, we are experiencing an annual employee turnover of about 12 per cent. Although this might not seem high at first glance, the industry standard is seven per cent. The principal objective of this report is to investigate the causes of employee engagement within the firm and, based on those, offer recommendations to improve the employees' experience of the workplace and increase employee retention.
simplified:
At Girox Foods, about 12% of our staff leave their jobs each year. This might not seem like a lot, but for our type of business, the normal number is 7%.

This report will look at why staff are happy or unhappy in our company. Then, it will suggest ways to make working here better for our employees and help more of them stay.
reference: At Girox Foods, around 12% of employees leave the company each year. This might not look high at first, but the normal level in the industy is about 7%. The main aim of this report is to study the reasons for employee engagement in the company. Based on those, give suggestions to make the workplace better and keep more employees.

original: Don't always follow positive feedback with negative feedback. When positive and negative feedback always appear to go hand in hand, the positives can become devalued and ignored. Ensure there are times when positive feedback is given for its own sake and resist the temptation to offer constructive criticism.
simplified: Don't always give good comments and then bad comments. If you always give good and bad comments together, the good ones might lose their value. People might ignore them. Sometimes, just give good comments. Don't always feel you need to give advice on how to improve.
reference: Don't always give negative feedback after positive feedback. If positive and negative comments always come together, the positive ones can lose their value and be ignored. Make sure you give positive feedback on its own, and avoid the urge to add criticism.

original: One of the most important modern functions of zoos is supporting international breeding programmes, particularly for endangered species. In the wild, some of the rarest species have difficulty in finding mates and breeding, and they might also be threatened by poachers, loss of their habitat and predators. A good zoo will enable these species to live and breed in a secure environment. In addition, as numbers of some wild species drop, there is an increased danger of populations becoming too genetically similar. Breeding programmes provide a safeguard: zoo-bred animals can be released into the wild to increase genetic diversity.
simplified:
One important job of zoos today is to help rare animals have babies. This is often done with animals from different countries.

In nature, it is hard for very rare animals to find partners and have babies. They are also in danger from hunters, losing their homes, and other animals.

Good zoos help these animals live safely and have babies in a safe place.

Also, when there are fewer wild animals, there is a danger that the animals will become too similar. This is not good for their health.

These breeding plans help protect animals. Animals born in zoos can go back to nature. This helps make the animal groups more varied and stronger.
reference: One of the most important roles of zoos is supporting international breeding programmes, especially for animals that are endangered. In the wild, some rare animals find it hard to find partners and have babies. They are also in danger from hunters, the loss of their homes, and other animals that hunt them. A good zoo gives these species a safe place to live and reproduce. Another problem is that when the number of animals in the wild becomes very small, they can become too genetically similar. Breeding programmes help with this, because animals born in zoos can later be relaesed into the wild to make the population stronger and more diverse.

original: The Scallion is printed weekly and distributed free in faculty buildings, with a readership of approximately 10,000 students. It is written and produced entirely by students. The survey shows that the newspaper is highly valued by university students and staff for entertainment, cultural enrichment and work experience. The cost of printing newspapers is significant. Furthermore, some students do not have easy access to the paper, since the only way to obtain a copy is to physically go to university. An additional environmental issue is that a large number of copies end up as litter on campus.
simplified:
The Scallion newspaper is printed every week. You can get it for free in university buildings. About 10,000 students read it. Students write and make the whole newspaper.

A survey shows that students and staff at the university like the newspaper a lot. They like it for fun, for learning about culture, and for getting work experience.

Printing the newspapers costs a lot of money. Also, some students cannot easily get the paper. This is because they have to go to the university to get a copy. Another problem is for the environment. Many copies are left as rubbish on campus.
reference: The Scallion is printed every week and given out for free in university buildings, with about 10,000 student readers. It is written and produced only by students. The survey shows that both students and staff value the paper for fun, culture, and work experience.However, printing the paper is expensive. Also, some students can not get it easily, as the only way to get a copy is to go to the university. Another problem is the environment: many copies are thrown away as rubbish on campus.

original: Spider venom is present in most species and serves the purpose of stunning or killing their prey rather than attacking humans. In fact, only 25 of the known spider species produce venom which can actually harm humans, and although spider bites can be painful, they are rarely deadly. Australia's notorious Sydney funnel-web spider has not produced any fatalities since anti-venom was developed in 1981. However, take care not to rub hairy spiders like tarantulas up the wrong way. When they feel in danger, they defend themselves by ejecting a cloud of urticating hairs. These irritating hairs then embed themselves in the skin or eyes of the attacker.
simplified:
Most spiders have venom. They use it to stun or kill their food, not to attack people.
Only 25 types of spiders we know have venom that can hurt humans.
Spider bites can be painful, but they are almost never deadly.
For example, the Sydney funnel-web spider in Australia is famous. It has not killed anyone since medicine for its bite was made in 1981.
But be careful not to make hairy spiders, like tarantulas, angry.
If they feel in danger, they protect themselves by throwing out a cloud of irritating hairs.
These hairs can then stick into your skin or eyes.
reference: Most spiders have venom, but it is mainly used to catch or kill their prey, not to attack humans. In fact, only 25 spider species are dangerous to people. Spider bites can hurt, but they almost never cause death. For example, Australia's famous Sydney funnel-web spider has not killed anyone since an anti-venom was created in 1981. You should be careful with hairy spiders like tarantulas.When they feel in danger, they release tiny sharp hairs that can stick in the skin or eyes of the attacker and cause irritation.

original: If we want to know where our capability for complex language came from, we need to look at how our brains are different from other animals. This relates to more than just brain size; it is important what other things our brains can do and when and why they evolved that way. And for this there are very few physical clues; artefacts left by our ancestors don't tell us what speech they were capable of making. One thing we can see in the remains of early humans, however, is the development of the mouth, throat and tongue. By about 100,000 years ago, humans had evolved the ability to create complex sounds. Before that, evolutionary biologists can only guess whether or not early humans communicated using more basic sounds.
simplified:
If we want to know how we learned to use difficult language, we must look at how our brains are not like other animals. It's not only about how big our brains are. It's also important what else our brains can do, and when and why they changed over time.

We have very few things to show us this. Old objects from our ancestors don't tell us what kind of speech they could make.

But we can see one thing in the bones of early humans: how their mouth, throat, and tongue grew. About 100,000 years ago, humans could make many different sounds. Before that time, scientists can only guess if early humans used simpler sounds to talk.
reference: If we want to know where our ability for complex language came from, we need to look at how the human brain is different from the brains of other animals. It is not only about brain size, but also about what our brains can do, when these abilities appreared and why. There are a few physical clues about this, because objects from early humans cannot show us what kind of speech thry used. But one thing we can study is the development of the mouth, throat and tongue. Around 100,000 years ago, humans developed the ability to make complex sounds. Before that, scientists could only guess if early humans used simpler sounds to communicate.

original: It is society, not nature, that tells us girls should favour arts and humanities and leave maths and physics to the boys. Coupled with this is the lack of positive female role models youngsters see doing science-related jobs. Cartoons and stories often show the crazy scientist, genius inventor, or adventurous astronaut as a man. Furthermore, there is an unfortunate perception that scientists are geeky, have poor social skills or that their work is lonely and detached from the rest of the world. These are false stereotypes portrayed by the media, but they may mean that girls do not identify with scientists, and see science as an unappealing career path. If girls saw more positive female role models in science it would give them more confidence and a greater sense of belonging in those subjects.
simplified:
Society, not nature, tells girls to like arts and humanities more, and boys to like maths and physics. Also, young people don't see many good examples of women working in science. Cartoons and stories often show the crazy scientist, clever inventor, or brave astronaut as a man.

People also wrongly think that scientists are strange, not good at talking to others, or that their work is lonely and separate from the world. These are wrong ideas shown by the media. They can make girls feel that they are not like scientists, and that science is not a good job for them.

If girls saw more good examples of women in science, they would feel more confident and feel like they belong in these subjects.
reference: It is society, not nature, that suggests girls should study arts and humanities while boys study maths and physics. Another problem is that young people do not often see positive female role models in science jobs. In cartoons and stories, the scientist, inventor, or astronaut is usually a man. There is also a negative idea that scientists are "geeky," have poor social skills, or work alone, far from the real world. These are false stereotypes shown by the media, but they may stop girls from seeing themselves as scientists and make science seem unattractive. If girls saw more positive female working in science, it would give them more confidence and help them feel that they belong in those subjects.

original: So much of what the speaker said rang true. I honestly believe there's a danger that the more connected we are, the more isolated we feel. I don't think this is such an issue for my generation who've lived without technology for so long. We know how to be alone and, more importantly, we know that it's OK to be alone. But the under 20s are another kettle of fish. They're so busy communicating that they never experience the feeling of solitude and run the risk of not learning how to enjoy their own company. In addition, they're learning conversation through messages that can be edited and changed at the expense of learning the art of real conversation in real time with the person in front of you.
simplified:
Many things the speaker said felt true. I really think there's a problem: the more we connect online, the more alone we feel. This is not a big problem for people my age. We lived without technology for a long time, so we know how to be alone, and we know it's okay.

But young people under 20 are very different. They are so busy talking online that they never have time alone. They might not learn to like being by themselves. Also, they learn to talk by sending messages that they can change. This means they don't learn how to have real conversations face-to-face with someone.
reference: Much of what the speaker said felt true to me. I believe there is a danger that the more connected we are, the more lonely we may feel. For my generation, this is less of a problem because we lived for many years without technology. We know how to spend time alone, and we know it is OK to be alone. But young people under 20 are different. They are always busy communicating, but they never really experience solitude. This means they may not learn how to enjoy being alone. Also, they are learning to talk through messages that can be edited, instead of learning real conversation in real time with another person in front of you.

original: Are things getting worse every day? Is progress an impossible goal? In Enlightenment Now, Steven Pinker looks at the big picture of human progress and finds good news. We are living longer, healthier, freer and happier lives. The real problem, Pinker argues, is that the Enlightenment values of reason and science are under attack. When commentators and demagogues appeal to people's tribalism, fatalism and distrust, then we are in danger of causing irreparable damage to important institutions like democracy and world co-operation.
simplified: Are things getting worse? Can we still make progress? In his book, Enlightenment Now, Steven Pinker looks at how humans have improved. He finds good news. We are living longer, healthier, freer, and happier lives. But Pinker says the real problem is that people are attacking important ideas. These ideas come from a time called the Enlightenment, and they are about using logic and science. When some leaders and writers try to make people think only about their own group, or believe nothing can change, or not trust others, we could badly damage important things like democracy and countries working together.
reference: Are things getting worse every day? Is progress impossible? In Enlightenment Now, Steven Pinker studies the history of human progress and finds much good news. People live longer, healthier, freer, and happier lives. But Pinker warns that the real danger is the attack on Enlightenment values such as reason and science. When leaders and commentators encourage people to think only of their own group, to give up hope, or to stop trusting others, we risk damaging democracy and world co-operation in a way that can't be fixed.

original: Wonder is New Yorker RJ Palacio's first novel. On her website, she explains that the idea for the book came to her after seeing a girl with facial deformities on the street one day. Wonder is RJ Palacio's first book.
She got the idea for the book.
She saw a girl on the street.
The girl's face looked different.
Wonder is a very popular book.
It sold many copies in America.
It has won many prizes.
Many schools use this book.
They talk about being mean to others.
They talk about friendship.
They talk about being different.
They are making a movie of the book.

reference: Wonder is the first book by RJ Palacio, a writer from New York. She got the idea after seeing a girl with a face that looked different. The book is very popular in the United States and has won many awards. Many schools use the book to talk about bullying, friendship, and being different. original: Chloe has two pet rats, Zena and Roxy. But she knows why people do not like them.

Her friend Martin had pet rats.

Chloe saw they were loving.

reference: Chloe has two pet rats, called Zena and Roxy. She knows that rats are not usual pets, and many people think they are dirty. Chloe often tells people that rats can be very good pets if you take care of them. She didn't like rats before, but her friend Martin showed her his rats. She saw they were kind and clever. original: Cape Town can be a dangerous place for baboons. Some have been injured or killed in car accidents and others have been electrocuted as they played with electric cables. Baboons are an endangered species and to save them and minimise conflicts between humans and baboons, the city council has employed a team of Baboon Monitors. The monitors' job is to chase baboons out of urban areas or catch them and release them in the countryside. This policy has had some success, though it is proving hard to stop baboons from coming back to the city once they see it as a source of easy food.
simplified:
Cape Town can be dangerous for baboons.
Cars hurt or kill some baboons.
Others touch electric wires.
They get a bad electric shock.
Not many baboons are left.
They are an endangered animal.
The city wants to save them.
They also want to stop problems.
Problems are between people and baboons.
So, the city hired a team.
These are Baboon Monitors.
Their job is to help.
They make baboons leave the city.
Or they catch them.
They take them to the country.
This plan helps a bit.
But it is hard.
Baboons come back to the city.
They find easy food there.

To help them, the city now has a team called Baboon Monitors. These people try to move baboons out of the city and take them back to the countryside. original: One of the most interesting cases of wild animals living in a city are the wild dogs of Moscow. In Moscow, there are approximately 35,000 wild dogs living on the streets. original: Your dreams might show you all kinds of insights into things that you didn't realise you were thinking about. Common dreams like being able to fly or falling, your teeth falling out or having no clothes on in a public place probably mean something similar in most people. But the key to understanding exactly what they mean to you is to connect them to the events and feelings in your daily life.
simplified:

reference: People have different dreams when they sleep. Some common dreams are flying, falling, losing teeth, or being outside with no clothes. These dreams often mean the same thing for many people. To know what your dream means, think about what is happening in your life and how you feel.

original: Social media, magazines and shop windows bombard people daily with things to buy, and British consumers are buying more clothes and shoes than ever before. original: Many city residents in Berlin, Germany complained that shooting pigs was unnecessarily cruel and there were heated arguments between hunters and animal lovers. original: I work for a global IT company, but because their headquarters is in the States, I do all my work online from home.
